title: How Applications Remember
description: What a product must remember and in what form. Learn the kinds of information applications store, how long each piece should live, and why storage is chosen based on how the product will find it again.

objectives.label: Distinguish the kinds of information an application stores, from records and relationships to files and events
Decide whether information should be temporary screen state, session state, persistent, or cached
Choose storage based on how the product will need to find the information again
Describe an information architecture clearly enough for a coding agent to build it

blocks.text:
Open a social post and it looks like one object: a video, a name, a caption, a like count, and comments. The video file does not contain the like count. The count comes from like relationships. The name comes from an account record. The caption comes from a post record. Each comment is its own record. Privacy rules decide whether this viewer may see the post at all.

The application is also keeping view events, recommendation signals, and often a temporary copy on the phone so the next open is faster. A file, a relationship, and a cached copy are not three ways of writing the same fact. They have different jobs, and they can be wrong independently: the phone can show an old count while the server already has a new one.

What looks like one post is assembled when you open it. The screen combines those pieces into one experience.

blocks.alt: One post screen beside the many kinds of stored information the application assembles it from
blocks.caption: One screen, many kinds of memory.
steps: Account record
Post record
Video file in file storage
Like and follow relationships
Comment records
View history events
Privacy rules
Recommendation information
Temporary cached copy on the phone

blocks.text:
Applications need different shapes of memory: individual values, structured records, collections, relationships, files, events, and sometimes meaning representations for search.

A record tells the system which fields belong to which thing. A relationship such as a Like connects two things without stuffing a full copy of every liked post into the user. A file lives in file storage while a database record remembers its name, owner, and location.

blocks.title: The catalog and the shelves
steps: A student uploads resume.pdf. The browser collects the file and shows upload progress.
File storage keeps the actual PDF bytes on the shelves.
A database record stores the file name, owner, upload date, type, storage location, and who may see it.
That record is the library catalog. It points to the file without stuffing the whole PDF into a small profile field.
Later retrieval uses the catalog first, then fetches the file from storage when the student or teacher opens it.

slides.title: What does a Save button store?

blocks.question: Five hundred students save the same opportunity. What should the application store?

options.label: A full copy of the opportunity inside each student's record
Five hundred relationships connecting each student to the same opportunity record
A new file for every save
Nothing until a student reloads the page

blocks.explanation: A save is a relationship: it connects a student and an opportunity and belongs to neither alone. Copying the whole opportunity into five hundred student records would create five hundred disconnected duplicates that can drift apart.

slides.title: The screen is not the data

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: A screen is not the data. It is a temporary presentation assembled from data.

You type a long comment, accidentally refresh the page, and it disappears. The comment existed, but only on the device. It was never saved. Every piece of information has a lifetime, and the product has to choose it.

Screen state covers unsaved form text, an open menu, or scroll position. Session state lasts across several actions, such as being logged in or a half-finished quiz, but may expire.

Persistent state must survive closing the browser, restarting the device, and switching phones. Ask: should this still exist after the page closes?

blocks.alt: Levels of information lifetime from temporary screen state through session state and persistent state, plus cache
blocks.caption: Ask: should this still exist after the page closes?
steps: Screen state: unsaved form text, an open menu, scroll position
Session state: being logged in, a shopping cart, a half-finished quiz
Persistent state: a published post, a submitted assignment, a grade
Cache: a fast temporary copy of information that officially lives elsewhere

blocks.text:
A cache is a temporary copy kept so a read is fast: the next videos queued before a swipe, album art, a like count already painted on the phone, or a common search result. The official likes still live in the relationships on the server. The copy on the phone can be missing, or it can be old.

If that copy disappears, the product should retrieve or rebuild from the real home. If the cache were the only copy, clearing the phone would delete the likes. A lifetime that is shorter than the fact's job is also why a draft vanishes on refresh, and why a submitted application must not live only in the open tab.

Speed is the reason to keep the copy. The official record is the reason you must be able to build the copy again.

blocks.question: A student submits an application. Tomorrow, on a different device, it must still be there. Which lifetime does the submission need?

options.label: Screen state, held in the open page
Persistent state, surviving restarts and device switches
Cache, because it is the fastest to read

blocks.explanation: A submission must survive refresh, restart, and switching devices, so it needs persistent state. Screen and session state expire too early, and a cache is only a rebuildable copy of something stored elsewhere.

slides.title: A fast copy, not the truth

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: A cache is not normally the official truth. It is a fast copy. If it disappears, the product should be able to retrieve or rebuild the information.

Do not start by asking which folder a fact goes in. Ask how the product will find it again, because that question decides what you store. Open project 847 is an exact lookup, so the project needs a stable id. Two students can both be named Maya, and a username can change. student_id does not change its meaning, so a relationship points at the id instead of the name.

A filter such as state equals Oklahoma, and the deadline has not passed, works only if those fields exist and mean one thing. Newest first works only if you stored a time. Show the people I follow works only if you stored the relationship, not a pasted copy of each profile. Text search and search by meaning need the words, or a representation of the meaning, prepared before the question arrives.

If the product cares what changed since the last login, something must have recorded when the change happened. Storage that cannot answer the product's questions is the wrong storage, even when every fact is technically saved somewhere.

blocks.alt: Six retrieval patterns: exact lookup by ID, filtering on fields, sorting and ranking, following relationships, text search, semantic search, and time-based retrieval
blocks.caption: If time matters to the product, the system must record time.
steps: Exact: open project 847 by its ID
Filter: state equals Oklahoma, deadline has not passed
Sort and rank: newest first, lowest price, highest score
Relationships: show the people I follow
Text search: documents containing the phrase water quality
Semantic: similar in meaning, even when the words differ
Time-based: what changed since the last login

blocks.text:
Exact facts such as county, age eligibility, and deadlines need structured filters. Similarity of meaning needs semantic search, which may use embeddings that place related ideas closer on a map of meaning.

Semantic similarity should never decide whether a deadline passed or a student is eligible. Filter first using facts. Rank or search using meaning.

slides.title: Filter the facts, rank the meaning

blocks.question: A student asks: find AI or data opportunities near Tulsa open to high school seniors. Which design answers it best?

options.label: Let semantic similarity decide whether the student is eligible
Apply structured filters for county, eligibility, and deadline, then rank the survivors by meaning
Store each opportunity as one long paragraph and scan it by hand
Look up each opportunity by exact ID

blocks.explanation: Exact facts such as county, age eligibility, and deadlines need structured filters. Similarity of meaning needs semantic search. Semantic similarity should never decide whether a deadline passed or a student is eligible.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Filter first using facts. Rank or search using meaning.

Telling an agent to build an app that uses a database forces it to guess the records, fields, relationships, files, events, and retrievals. Naming them turns a guess into a build.

Say what each record holds, how long it lives, how it will be found again, and which work runs on the device versus a server. An AI model does not automatically remember a student or a past recommendation. The application must retrieve the saved context and send it to the model.

You do not need to memorize database brands. You need to see information clearly enough that an agent is not inventing your architecture.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: You do not need to memorize database technology. You need to learn to see information clearly. Without those decisions, the agent is only guessing.
